articles.headlineTranslated: Measles confirmed in Ehime for the first time in 14 years: The basics of measles and the effectiveness of vaccination you should know, explained by Director Hiroto Shinomiya of the Ehime Prefectural Institute of Public Health and Environmental Research.
articles.summary: Three measles cases were confirmed in Ehime Prefecture as of November 26, 2026, the first in the region since 2012 (14 years). Nationwide, 582 cases had been recorded as of November 18, 2026, more than double the 265 cases in 2013. Dr. Hiroto Shinomiya, director of the Ehime Prefectural Institute of Public Health and Environmental Research, explains measles’ high contagion with about a 10-day incubation, initial fever, cough and runny nose, then fever above 39°C and rash after 2–3 days, and potential complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, including death. There is no specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive. Vaccination is highlighted as protective, and Ehime Prefecture advises individuals with suspected measles to contact healthcare providers before visiting. The article delivers the basics of measles and vaccination effectiveness as public health guidance.

articles.headlineTranslated: Yokohama City University Identifies Nectin-4 as the Major Entry Receptor for Rubella Virus.
articles.summary: Rubella virus uses Nectin-4 as the major host cell entry receptor, a finding by a Yokohama City University–led team published in Nature (November 2026). Using rubella virus–like particles and CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screens, they show Nectin-4 mediates entry in airway epithelial cells and placental syncytiotrophoblasts. In air–liquid interface airway models, rubella infects from the basal surface and releases progeny apically; infection is markedly reduced by Nectin-4 inhibition. Placental organoids reveal high Nectin-4 on syncytiotrophoblast surfaces, with infection suppressed by Nectin-4–blocking antibodies. Notably, Nectin-4 is also a measles virus receptor, suggesting shared host factors across these distinct viruses. This discovery advances understanding of rubella airway shedding and maternal–fetal transmission and may inform antiviral or vaccine strategies against congenital rubella syndrome. Background: global congenital rubella cases around 30,000/year (2019).
